clue.text: Hedges unlikely to be planted in drained swamps

indicators.note: something planted in the ground sits inside it, so one piece goes into another
a drained thing has had its contents emptied, leaving only the shell of first and last letters

parts.note: the word with its middle emptied out
a tall story is an unlikely one

explanation.surface: A gardener warns that hedgerows will not take if planted in reclaimed marshland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hedges' looks like a noun for garden plants, but it is a verb: someone who hedges avoids giving a straight answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hedge is to play for time and evade commitment, which is exactly what someone does when delaying tactically.

clue.text: Dye cutting-edge coats

indicators.note: a coat wraps around what lies beneath it, so the letters sit covered inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the hyphen, from inside the first word into the second

explanation.surface: An advert for the latest high-tech paint or dye used as a coating.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen joins the two halves of the hidden run: cut-TING-E-dge.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean to give something a slight colour, or the colour itself, as when fabric picks up a faint hue.

clue.text: Freshen up new house at first for lender

indicators.note: placed at first means this piece is put at the front of the answer

parts.note: Libra is one of the twelve houses (signs) of the zodiac

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: to air a room is to freshen it
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Advice to redecorate a new home first in order to satisfy a mortgage lender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freshen up' reads as one phrasal verb, but 'up' is separately the reversal signal. The 'house' is astrological, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A librarian runs a lending library and hands out books on loan, so the job is to lend.

clue.text: Grand picture house graduate leaves about six, initially uplifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, uplifted means the assembled letters are read from the bottom upwards
the graduate leaves, so those letters are dropped from the picture house

parts.note: a picture house is a cinema
an MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate
C is short for circa, Latin for about

indicators.note: initially picks out the first letter of the following word

parts.note: the first letter of six

explanation.surface: A grand cinema loses a graduate employee around six o'clock and is somehow lifted up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' drops MA from CINEMA to give CINE; add C (about) and S ('six, initially'), giving CINECS, and 'uplifted' turns that upside down in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Scenery that is grand or impressive to look at is described as scenic, so the adjective fits a grand view.

clue.text: Elusive ginger cat in hole near motorway area

indicators.note: near means next to, so these pieces sit side by side

parts.note: M as in the M1, a British motorway
A is the abbreviation for area
a cavity is a hole or hollow

explanation.surface: A stray ginger cat has hidden itself in a hole beside the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat reads as being in the hole, but 'in' only links; the hole is merely beside the motorway area in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Macavity is the Mystery Cat of T. S. Eliot's poems, a ginger criminal mastermind who is never found at the scene.

clue.text: Single mum ran into bar upset with me

indicators.note: something upset has been knocked over and left in a mess, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lone mother storms into a pub, angry with the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single mum' reads as one phrase, but 'Single' alone is the definition, meaning a record released on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan's song was released as a hit record, famously by the Byrds, so it is an example of a pop record release.

clue.text: Chic covering one fine group

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap around it on the outside

parts.note: classy means stylish or chic
the Roman numeral for one
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Fashion talk: a stylish outfit covering one elegant group of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'group' looks like a noun, but it is a verb here: to sort things into categories.
explanation.definitionFit: To group items is to sort them into categories by shared features, which is what sorting into classes means.

clue.text: Binary digital message?

parts.note: surface reading: a string of ones and zeros sent by computer; setter's reading: a gesture made with two fingers (digits), carrying a clear meaning

explanation.walkthrough: The computing words hide their plain senses: binary means twofold and digital means done with the fingers. In Britain the gesture, palm inward, is a rude insult.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-fingered hand gesture signalling victory or, reversed, contempt, is literally a communication made with a pair of digits.

clue.text: Pick out a cracking Archer character

indicators.note: cracking something open lets a piece get in between its parts

parts.note: William Tell, the legendary Swiss archer
a part is a character played by an actor
taken as written

explanation.surface: Spot a notable character from The Archers, the long-running BBC radio soap.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital A invites The Archers, a BBC radio soap set in farming country, but the archer is William Tell.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick someone out from a crowd is to distinguish them, the idiomatic sense of discriminating between similar things.

clue.text: Insane habit abroad, losing sight of hotel while away

indicators.note: abroad, in the sense of all over the place, tells us the letters are scattered into a new order
losing sight of something means it goes missing, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A crazy habit picked up overseas makes someone forget the hotel while travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing sight of' removes the H of hotel from INSANE HABIT, and 'abroad' rearranges the remaining ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In absentia is Latin for 'in absence', used of something done to a person who is away, such as a trial.

clue.text: Troubles doctor not to join in with exercises

indicators.note: the doctor declining to join in means those letters are absent from the exercises

parts.note: drills are training exercises

explanation.surface: A doctor who refuses to join in workouts causes trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not to join in with' takes DR (doctor) out of DRILLS (exercises).
explanation.definitionFit: Ills are misfortunes or problems, so the plural noun matches troubles.

clue.text: Star writing at home about strict regimen

parts.note: Vega is a bright star in the constellation Lyra

indicators.note: turning about means facing the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: MS is manuscript, a piece of writing
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A celebrity writes a book at home about following a strict diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' suggests a celebrity, but it is a real star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Veganism excludes all animal products from diet and lifestyle, a demanding regime of rules to follow.

clue.text: Wrong headings in report? This shouldn't be wrong in the paper!

definitions.text: This shouldn't be wrong in the paper

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the words are said out loud

parts.note: a sin is a wrong; tacks are headings or courses in sailing

explanation.surface: Mistaken headlines in a newspaper report; they should not be wrong in print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'headings' suggests newspaper titles, but in sailing a tack is the direction a boat is heading.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar and sentence structure should be correct in a printed newspaper; errors in word order are the proofreader's concern.

clue.text: Mystic provided with universal awareness at last after setback

indicators.note: a setback sets things going backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: if means provided that
U is the film certificate for universal

indicators.note: at last points at the final letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A mystic who has gained universal awareness at last after a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'provided with' reads as 'given', but 'provided' alone means if, and 'with' only links it to the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sufi is a follower of the mystical tradition of Islam, seeking direct experience of the divine.

clue.text: Order boring new clue to be changed as not acceptable

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into something, so one piece goes inside
letters that are changed have been altered and rearranged into another sequence

parts.note: taken as written
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: An instruction that a dull new clue must be rewritten because it will not pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like a verdict on the clue, but it means drilling into. OM, the Order of Merit, is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unwelcome is not wanted or received gladly, so it is unwanted and cannot be accepted.

clue.text: Hop in the middle following foxtrot and interrupt ball

indicators.note: what is in the middle is the central letter of the word

parts.note: the central letter
f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
Foxtrot is F in the phonetic alphabet
to break in is to interrupt

explanation.surface: Dance-floor talk: a hop, a foxtrot, then cutting in at a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ball' looks like the dance, but it is a cricket delivery. Hop and foxtrot also pull toward dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, an off break is a delivery bowled by a spinner that turns from the off side into the batter.

clue.text: Day after day, soldier accompanies lady on vacation

indicators.note: to accompany is to go alongside, so the pieces sit together

parts.note: a regular is a professional soldier in the standing army

indicators.note: a place on vacation has been vacated and emptied, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: the word with its middle emptied

explanation.surface: Every day a soldier escorts a woman who is on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' reads as being on holiday, but it means emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something day after day means doing it at fixed, frequent intervals, the adverb of habitual routine.

clue.text: Matey and reportedly drunk, make an amorous gesture

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, and drunk means slurred, so the words are heard as a tipsy person would say them

parts.note: to blow a kiss, as slurred by someone who has had too much

explanation.surface: A pally, tipsy person blowing kisses at someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The drunken slur turns the S of kiss into SH. A bloke is British slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Blokeish means hearty and laddish in manner, the friendly male camaraderie that matey also describes.

clue.text: Contemptible person taking in adult now and then, right?

definitions.text: Contemptible person taking in adult now and then, right?

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a swine is a nasty, contemptible person

indicators.note: now and then means only occasionally, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A rogue who occasionally cheats grown-ups: surely that's right?
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also describes the answer: a despicable person who takes in, or dupes, a grown-up from time to time.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone in is to deceive them, and a cheat who deceives people for gain is a contemptible fraudster.

clue.text: Greedily eat tripe?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to gorge on food, a British slang verb
second meaning: animal stomach and intestines, the offal sold as tripe

explanation.walkthrough: Tripe, cooked cow's stomach, is here taken literally as innards; the question mark flags that it is only an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Guts means both the entrails of an animal and, in informal British use, to eat food greedily.

clue.text: Feature of fancy cravat Charlie put aside for American

indicators.note: fancy, as an adjective meaning elaborate or contrived, tells us the letters are reworked
Charlie is put aside to make room for American, so one letter replaces the other

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A detail of a flashy necktie that Charlie set aside in favour of something American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put aside for' swaps the C of CRAVAT for A, giving ARAVAT, which 'fancy' rearranges. 'Feature' is a feature film: Avatar is James Cameron's 2009 blockbuster.
explanation.definitionFit: Avatar is the title of a famous full-length film, and a full-length film is called a feature.

clue.text: Sweetheart briefly in thrall to drink, missing Eastern European

indicators.note: missing means Eastern is absent, so that letter is removed
being in thrall to something is being held within its grip, so the shortened word goes inside

parts.note: sake is Japanese rice wine

indicators.note: briefly means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: a love is a sweetheart

explanation.surface: A lover is gripped by drink while missing someone from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts LOVE to LOV, which goes 'in thrall to' SAKE, giving SLOVAKE; 'missing Eastern' then drops the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: A Slovak is a native of Slovakia, a country in central Europe, so is one example of a European.

clue.text: Byron delivered this extract from overseas

indicators.note: an extract is a piece taken out of a longer text

parts.note: the letters sit in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: Lord Byron sent a passage of writing home from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron did write much of his work abroad, so 'from overseas' reads as fact rather than the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron was a Romantic poet, so what he produced was poetry, written in lines of metre.

clue.text: King, perhaps with knight, arranged violets

indicators.note: flowers that are arranged are set out in a new order

parts.note: N is the chess notation for knight
taken as written

explanation.surface: A king and a knight arranging flowers, or chess pieces beside a vase of violets.
explanation.walkthrough: King and knight pull toward chess or royalty, but King is Stephen King, the horror writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen King writes best-selling fiction books, so he is one example of an author of long fiction.

clue.text: Saint Nick is one in no hurry

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for saint
to nick and to nail both mean to catch or arrest

explanation.surface: Father Christmas, Saint Nicholas, is never rushed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint Nick' reads as Santa Claus, but the two words split: nick is British slang for arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: The snail is proverbially the slowest of creatures, so it is the example of something that never rushes.

clue.text: Square in France — visit when temperature's dropped

indicators.note: France goes in where the dropped letter was, so it is the replacement
temperature's letter being dropped means it leaves the word

parts.note: a tour is a visit around a place
T is the abbreviation for temperature
F is the international vehicle code for France

explanation.surface: A town square in France is worth a visit once the heat has gone down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped' removes the T of TOUR and 'in' puts F (France) in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: Four is the square of two, so a square number can be the answer; 'square' is not the town square of the surface.

clue.text: This writer's flannel quite possibly irrelevant

parts.note: the writer referring to themself: I am, shortened
flannel is one kind of cloth, hence 'quite possibly'

explanation.surface: A writer admits their own waffle is probably beside the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flannel' suggests waffle, British slang for empty talk, but it is the woollen fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immaterial has no bearing on the matter at hand, so it does not matter and is beside the point.

clue.text: Two leading tenors sing outside hospital for charity show

parts.note: the two leading letters of tenors

indicators.note: outside means the confession wraps around the hospital letter

parts.note: to sing, in slang, is to confess, to let on
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Two star tenors give voice around a hospital to raise money for charity.
explanation.walkthrough: TE comes from the first two letters of tenors. 'Sing' in the informer's sense is LET ON, which goes 'outside' H.
explanation.definitionFit: A telethon is a long televised broadcast that raises money for a good cause, a type of charity show.

clue.text: Maybe princes greatly impress old Republican, on reflection

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front

parts.note: to slay an audience is to impress them hugely
O is the abbreviation for old
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: Perhaps princes can win over an old republican opponent, once he thinks it over.
explanation.walkthrough: Princes and a republican set up a political scene, but the words are just letter sources.
explanation.definitionFit: Princes are members of a ruling family, so they are examples of members of a monarchy.
